families.name: Ubuntu
families.blurb: Canonical's Ubuntu ships every April and October, with a long-term support (LTS) release every April of an even year.
families.cadence: Every 6 months (April and October). LTS every 2 years.

source.label: Ubuntu release team: list of releases

families.about: Ubuntu is made by Canonical and is one of the most used Linux distributions on desktops, servers and in the cloud. It is based on Debian. Every April and October brings a new version; the April release of even-numbered years is a long-term support (LTS) release that most people use.

editions.name: Ubuntu Desktop
editions.desc: The main edition, with the GNOME desktop.

editions.name: Ubuntu Server
editions.desc: No desktop; for servers, VMs and the cloud.

editions.name: Kubuntu
editions.desc: Official flavor with the KDE Plasma desktop.

editions.name: Xubuntu
editions.desc: Official flavor with the light Xfce desktop.

editions.name: Lubuntu
editions.desc: Official flavor with LXQt, for older or low-memory PCs.

editions.name: Ubuntu MATE
editions.desc: Official flavor with the classic MATE desktop.

editions.name: Ubuntu Budgie
editions.desc: Official flavor with the Budgie desktop.

editions.name: Ubuntu Studio
editions.desc: Official flavor for audio, video and graphics work.

faq.q: What is the difference between Ubuntu LTS and interim releases?
faq.a: An LTS (long-term support) release comes every two years in April and gets five years of updates, up to ten with Ubuntu Pro. Interim releases come every April and October in between and are supported for nine months.

faq.q: Which Ubuntu version should I install?
faq.a: Most people should install the newest LTS release for stability. Choose the newest interim release if you want newer software and are happy to upgrade every six months.

families.name: Fedora
families.blurb: Fedora Linux ships about every 6 months, usually around April/May and October/November, and often slips by a week or two.
families.cadence: About every 6 months. Slips of 1-2 weeks are common.
families.about: Fedora Linux is a community distribution sponsored by Red Hat, known for shipping new technology early. Fedora Workstation uses the GNOME desktop. Each version is supported until about four weeks after the release two versions later, so roughly 13 months.

editions.name: Fedora Workstation
editions.desc: The main desktop edition, with GNOME.

editions.name: Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop
editions.desc: Desktop edition with KDE Plasma.

editions.name: Fedora Server
editions.desc: For servers, without a desktop.

editions.name: Fedora Silverblue
editions.desc: Atomic (image-based) desktop with GNOME.

editions.name: Fedora Kinoite
editions.desc: Atomic (image-based) desktop with KDE Plasma.

editions.name: Fedora Cloud
editions.desc: Images for cloud servers and VMs.

editions.name: Fedora IoT
editions.desc: For devices and edge computing.

editions.name: Fedora Spins
editions.desc: Other desktops: Xfce, Cinnamon, LXQt, MATE and more.

faq.q: How long is a Fedora release supported?
faq.a: Until about four weeks after the release that comes two versions later, so roughly 13 months. Fedora 44, for example, is supported until 2 June 2027.

faq.q: What is the difference between Fedora Workstation and Silverblue?
faq.a: Both use GNOME. Silverblue is an atomic (image-based) version: the system updates as one unit that can be rolled back, and apps are installed as Flatpaks.

families.name: Debian
families.blurb: Debian stable releases come roughly every 2 years, when the project decides the testing branch is ready.
families.cadence: About every 2 years, with no fixed date.
families.about: Debian is one of the oldest Linux distributions, run by volunteers. Ubuntu, Linux Mint and many others are built on it. Debian releases a new stable version roughly every two years, when it is ready rather than on a fixed date.

editions.name: Network installer (netinst)
editions.desc: Small image; pick your desktop during installation. The usual choice.

editions.name: Live images
editions.desc: Try Debian with GNOME, KDE, Xfce and others before installing.

editions.name: All downloads
editions.desc: Full images, other architectures and mirrors.

faq.q: What are Debian stable, testing and unstable?
faq.a: Stable is the released version (Debian 13 "trixie" today). Testing is the next release while it is being built (Debian 14 "forky"). Unstable, called sid, is where new packages arrive first.

faq.q: How long is a Debian release supported?
faq.a: About three years of full security support from the Debian security team, then Debian LTS extends it to about five years in total.

families.name: Linux Mint
families.blurb: Linux Mint follows the Ubuntu LTS base. The team has said it is moving to a longer development cycle.
families.cadence: Changing: previously twice a year, now about once a year (reported).
families.about: Linux Mint is a beginner-friendly desktop distribution built on Ubuntu's long-term support releases. It comes in Cinnamon, MATE and Xfce editions, and there is also LMDE, an edition based directly on Debian.

editions.name: Cinnamon Edition
editions.desc: The flagship edition, with the Cinnamon desktop.

editions.name: Xfce Edition
editions.desc: Lighter edition for older computers.

editions.name: MATE Edition
editions.desc: Classic, steady desktop.

editions.name: LMDE
editions.desc: Linux Mint Debian Edition: Cinnamon on a Debian base.

faq.q: Which Linux Mint edition should I choose?
faq.a: Cinnamon is the main and most popular edition. Xfce is lighter and suits older computers. MATE is a classic, steady desktop.
Linux Mint Debian Edition: the same Cinnamon desktop built directly on Debian instead of Ubuntu.

families.name: GNOME
families.blurb: The GNOME desktop ships every March and September on a published calendar with alpha, beta and release-candidate dates.
families.about: GNOME is the desktop environment you see in Fedora Workstation, Ubuntu and Debian's default install. You do not download GNOME on its own: you get a new GNOME version when your distribution ships it.

faq.q: How do I check which GNOME version I have?
faq.a: Open Settings and go to the About page (under System in recent versions); it shows the GNOME version.
Since GNOME 40 in 2021, each release gets the next whole number. Two come out each year, in March and September.

families.name: Linux kernel
families.blurb: A new mainline kernel arrives every 9-10 weeks: a two-week merge window, then weekly release candidates (rc1, rc2 and so on) until Linus Torvalds calls it final.
families.about: The Linux kernel is the core of every Linux system, led by Linus Torvalds. Most people get new kernels through their distribution's updates; kernel.org publishes the source code for each release.

editions.name: Stable kernel
editions.desc: The newest release, with bug-fix updates.

editions.name: Longterm (LTS) kernels
editions.desc: Older kernels kept up to date for years.

editions.name: Mainline (release candidates)
editions.desc: The next kernel while it is being tested.

faq.q: Which Linux kernel version should I use?
faq.a: Use the kernel your distribution ships. If you need long support, pick a longterm (LTS) kernel such as 6.18 instead of the newest one.

faq.q: What is a kernel release candidate (rc)?
faq.a: After a two-week merge window for new features, Linus Torvalds releases weekly test versions called rc1, rc2 and so on. The final kernel usually follows rc7, or rc8 if more fixes are needed.

families.name: KDE Plasma
families.blurb: KDE Plasma is the desktop of Kubuntu, Fedora KDE, KDE neon and many others. A new feature release comes about every four months, followed by weekly and then monthly bug-fix updates.
families.cadence: About every 4 months (February, June, October), on a published schedule.
families.about: KDE Plasma is a highly customizable desktop environment made by the KDE community, which turned 30 in October 2026. Like GNOME, you get Plasma through a distribution: Kubuntu, Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop and KDE neon ship it by default. Some versions, like Plasma 6.6, are long-term support releases.

editions.name: KDE neon
editions.desc: KDE's own showcase system with the newest Plasma.

editions.name: Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop
editions.desc: Fedora's Plasma edition; gets new Plasma versions quickly.

editions.name: Kubuntu
editions.desc: Ubuntu's official Plasma flavor.

editions.name: More distributions
editions.desc: KDE's list of distributions that ship Plasma.

faq.q: What is a Plasma LTS release?
faq.a: Some Plasma versions are long-term support releases that keep getting bug fixes after newer versions are out. Plasma 6.6 is supported until August 2029.

faq.q: Does KDE Plasma still support X11?
faq.a: With Plasma 6.8, starting X11 sessions is being retired and Plasma runs on Wayland. Older X11 apps still run through XWayland.

families.name: NixOS
families.blurb: NixOS is a Linux distribution where the whole system is described in configuration files. It releases twice a year, in May and November, and each version is supported for about seven months.
families.cadence: Twice a year: end of May and end of November (version numbers YY.05 and YY.11).
families.about: NixOS is built on the Nix package manager: you describe your whole system in one configuration and can roll back any change. New versions come out at the end of May and the end of November, and the previous version stays supported for one more month.

editions.name: Graphical installer
editions.desc: Live image with a desktop and an installer (GNOME or Plasma).

editions.name: Minimal installer
editions.desc: Command-line image for experienced users and servers.

editions.name: Nix package manager
editions.desc: Use Nix on any Linux distribution or macOS.

faq.q: How long is a NixOS release supported?
faq.a: About seven months. Each release stays supported for one month after the next one comes out, so you have time to upgrade.

faq.q: What do NixOS version numbers mean?
faq.a: They are the year and month of the release: 26.05 came out in May 2026 and 26.11 is planned for November 2026.

families.name: Firefox
families.blurb: Mozilla Firefox gets a new major version every two weeks on a published release calendar, plus an Extended Support Release (ESR) for organisations that want fewer changes.
families.cadence: Every 2 weeks, on dates Mozilla publishes in advance.
families.about: Firefox is the open-source web browser made by Mozilla and the default browser on Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian and many other distributions. A new major version ships every two weeks; most Linux users get it automatically through their distribution, Flatpak or Snap.

editions.name: Firefox
editions.desc: The regular release, updated every two weeks.

editions.name: Firefox ESR
editions.desc: Extended Support Release: fewer changes, for organisations.

editions.name: Beta, Developer Edition, Nightly
editions.desc: Try the next versions early.

editions.name: Firefox on Flathub
editions.desc: Install as a Flatpak on any distribution.

faq.a: The Extended Support Release gets new features only about once a year but receives security fixes in between. Organisations use it for fewer changes; the current ESR is Firefox 153.
A new major version ships every two weeks, on dates Mozilla publishes in its release calendar, with smaller fix releases in between when needed.

releases.summary: Ubuntu 27.04 is the next regular Ubuntu release after 26.10. It is a short-term release, supported for 9 months.

evidence.text: Released on its scheduled date of 15 October 2026.
Reported to ship with the GNOME 51 desktop and a Linux 7.x kernel.

sources.label: Ubuntu release team: list of releases

highlights.title: Linux 7.3 kernel
highlights.text: Includes early support for Snapdragon X2 Elite laptops among other hardware changes since 26.04 LTS.

releases.summary: Fedora 45 was released on Nov 3, 2026. Our forecast from before the release is kept on this page for the record.

evidence.text: Fedora 45 beta shipped.
The 20 October final release was reported as a no-go and slipped.
Fedora's go/no-go moved the target to 27 October.
One later article gives 3 November. We could not reach Fedora's schedule page to confirm, so this stays a prediction.
Fedora Bodhi (official update system) lists Fedora 45 as released on Nov 3, 2026.

forecast.summary: Fedora 45 has slipped past its first target date. Sources disagree on the new date, so we show a window instead of a single day.

highlights.title: New console with kmscon
highlights.text: The legacy in-kernel console is replaced by kmscon, with smoother rendering and better Unicode and font support.

highlights.title: Signed packages required
highlights.text: Packages now need a valid signature by default before they can be installed.

highlights.title: One secrets service
highlights.text: Desktop password storage is standardised on oo7, replacing backends such as GNOME Keyring and KWallet.

highlights.title: Newer tools
highlights.text: Python 3.15, Go 1.27, GCC 16.2, glibc 2.44 and Podman 6, plus a new web installer flow for Atomic Desktops.

highlightsSource.label: Fedora Magazine: Fedora Linux 45 Beta announcement (features as announced for the beta)

evidence.text: Fedora 44 shipped on 28 April 2026, about six months before Fedora 45.
We found no official Fedora 46 date. Our window comes from Fedora's usual six-month gap, plus allowance for slips.
Fedora Bodhi (official update system) lists Fedora 46 as in development (not released yet).

releases.summary: Debian 14 "forky" has no release date. Debian releases a new stable version about every two years, which points to mid-2027 or later.

evidence.text: Debian 13 "trixie" was released on 9 August 2025.
A community-maintained estimate puts the freeze around 15 March 2027. It is not an official Debian date.
Debian's two-year cadence from August 2025 points to mid-to-late 2027. The next release after forky is named "duke".

The rename from 23 to 27 and the "Adrien" codename come from a single source, so we treat them as unconfirmed.

releases.summary: GNOME 52 is the next GNOME desktop release after GNOME 51.

evidence.text: The GNOME release calendar lists alpha on 9 January, beta on 30 January, release candidate on 27 February and final on 17 March 2027.

releases.summary: GNOME 51 "A Coruña" is the current GNOME desktop, released on 16 September 2026. It reaches you through your distribution, for example Ubuntu 26.10 and Fedora 45.

evidence.text: GNOME 51 was released on 16 September 2026.

highlights.title: Smoother desktop
highlights.text: Improved frame scheduling keeps animations smooth even when the system is busy.

highlights.title: Settings
highlights.text: Auto Rotate for devices with an accelerometer, better display arrangement and DNS search domains in network settings.

highlights.title: Remote Desktop
highlights.text: You can now pass your smartcard through to the remote computer, for example a workplace sign-in card.

highlights.title: Files and accessibility
highlights.text: A drag counter badge in Files, smarter selection, and Reduced Motion respected in many more places.

releases.summary: Linux 7.4 should arrive in the last week or two of December 2026, after a normal merge window and seven or eight release candidates.

evidence.text: Linux 7.3 was released on 18 October 2026.
A two-week merge window plus seven weekly release candidates gives 20 December. An rc8 would push it to 27 December. Most kernels ship after rc7.
Linux kernel 7.4 rc1 was tagged on Nov 1, 2026 (kernel.org releases feed).

releases.summary: Linux 7.5 follows 7.4 by about 9-10 weeks, which points to late February or early March 2027.

evidence.text: Adding 9-10 weeks to our Linux 7.4 window gives 21 February to 7 March 2027. The window widens with every release candidate that slips.

releases.summary: Linux 7.3 is the newest stable Linux kernel, released on 18 October 2026. The latest bug-fix update is 7.3.1, and Ubuntu 26.10 ships it.

evidence.text: Linux 7.3 was released on 18 October 2026.

highlights.title: Better VRAM sharing
highlights.text: GPUs with little video memory share it more fairly when several apps compete for it.

highlights.title: sched_ext sub-schedulers
highlights.text: Each cgroup can now run its own BPF-based task scheduler.

highlights.title: New sandboxing
highlights.text: A new failfs file system plus fchroot(2) gives a simple way to lock processes down.

highlights.title: Faster storage
highlights.text: Btrfs and Ext4 performance improvements, and faster FUSE over io_uring.

releases.type: Long-term support (5 years, 10 with Ubuntu Pro)
releases.summary: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS "Resolute Raccoon" is the current long-term support release, out since 23 April 2026. It gets security updates until April 2031, or ten years with Ubuntu Pro, which makes it the version most people should install.

specs.v: Until April 2031 (10 years with Ubuntu Pro)
2 GHz dual-core CPU, 6 GB RAM, 25 GB disk

highlights.title: Five years of updates
highlights.text: As an LTS release it receives security updates and critical fixes for five years, until April 2031; Ubuntu Pro extends this to ten years.

highlights.title: Upgrade path from 24.04 LTS
highlights.text: Most Ubuntu users move from one LTS to the next every two years; 26.04 is the upgrade target for Ubuntu 24.04 LTS "Noble Numbat".

highlights.title: Higher desktop requirements
highlights.text: Canonical recommends a 2 GHz dual-core CPU, 6 GB of RAM and 25 GB of disk; lighter flavors like Xubuntu or Lubuntu run on 2 GB.

evidence.text: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS was released on 23 April 2026 (Ubuntu upgrade metadata and endoflife.date agree).
The first point release, 26.04.1, came out on 27 August 2026.

releases.summary: Debian 13 "trixie" is the current stable Debian release, out since 9 August 2025. It gets five years of support from Debian's security and long-term support teams, and the latest point release is 13.7.

specs.v: GNOME 48, KDE Plasma 6.3, Xfce 4.20, LXQt 2.1.0 and more
Until 9 Aug 2028, then LTS until 30 Jun 2030

highlights.title: Updated desktops
highlights.text: Ships GNOME 48, KDE Plasma 6.3, Xfce 4.20, LXQt 2.1.0 and other desktop environments.

highlights.title: Ready for 2038
highlights.text: Every architecture except i386 now uses a 64-bit time_t, so dates beyond 2038 work.

highlights.title: Reproducible builds
highlights.text: Big progress towards packages that build byte-for-byte the same; a new debian-repro-status tool shows the status on your system.

highlights.title: Huge archive
highlights.text: 69,830 packages, over 14,100 of them new, and more than 63% of packages updated since Debian 12.

evidence.text: Debian announced Debian 13 "trixie" as its new stable release on 9 August 2025, after 2 years, 1 month and 30 days of development.
Point release 13.7 came out on 12 September 2026 (Debian archive Release file).

releases.summary: Linux Mint 22.3 "Zena" is the current Linux Mint release, out since 11 January 2026. It is a long-term support release based on Ubuntu 24.04 and is supported until April 2029.

highlights.title: Long-term support
highlights.text: Supported until April 2029, like every Linux Mint 22.x release.

highlights.title: Ubuntu 24.04 base
highlights.text: Linux Mint 22.x is built on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, so it shares its hardware support and package base.

highlights.title: Easy move from 22.x
highlights.text: People on Linux Mint 22, 22.1 or 22.2 can move to 22.3 through the Update Manager.

evidence.text: endoflife.date lists Linux Mint 22.3 "Zena" as released on 11 January 2026.
Linux Mint's release notes call 22.3 a long-term support release supported until April 2029, based on Ubuntu 24.04.

releases.summary: KDE Plasma 6.8, the "30th Anniversary Edition", came out on 14 October 2026, KDE's 30th birthday. It retires X11 sessions in favour of Wayland and adds a dwell clicker, better remote desktop and screen recording with audio. The latest bug-fix update is 6.8.2.

highlights.title: Wayland only
highlights.text: After 42 years of the X Window System, starting X11 sessions in Plasma is being retired.

highlights.title: Dwell clicker
highlights.text: A new accessibility feature clicks for you when the pointer stops moving, with no extra app needed.

highlights.title: Better remote desktop
highlights.text: Much better performance and quality from Plasma's built-in remote desktop server.

highlights.title: Recording with audio
highlights.text: Spectacle can record system audio and the microphone together, so you can narrate screen recordings.

evidence.text: KDE announced Plasma 6.8, the "30th Anniversary Edition", on 14 October 2026.
endoflife.date lists 6.8.2 as the latest bug-fix update, released 27 October 2026.

The schedule moves the Plasma 6.6.8 LTS update two weeks earlier, to 16 February 2027, so it does not clash with 6.9.0.

highlights.title: Native systemd boot options

evidence.text: endoflife.date lists NixOS 26.05 "Yarara" as released on 30 May 2026, supported until 31 December 2026.
